newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bank branch numbers fall 10 pct in 1996 - KPMG.
newsitem.headline: NZ bank branch numbers fall 10 pct in 1996 - KPMG.

text.p: The number of bank branches fell nearly 10 percent last year as electronic banking became more popular with consumers, according to a review of the industry by accountancy firm KPMG published on Wednesday.
Andrew Dinsdale, chairman of KPMG's banking and finance group, said the company's review of the banking sector showed overall branch numbers had fallen 134 to 1,293.
Despite the large fall in branch numbers, bank profits last year were virtually unchanged from 1995.
Of the main trading banks, only WestpacTrust increased its branch numbers in the past year, and that was only due to its merger with Trust Bank.
Now the largest bank here, WestpacTrust has 404 branches. Westpac and Trust Bank had 416 branches before they merged.
Bank of New Zealand and ANZ-PostBank trimmed their branch numbers by 42 and 73 respectively, KPMG said in its survey of banking performances released today.
National Bank has four fewer branches than a year ago, and ASB Bank two.
Dinsdale said the increasing popularity of electronic banking had caused some branch closures and would lead to more in the future, particularly with intensive competition.
"While New Zealand still has one of the highest ratios of bank branches per head of population in the world, further rationalisation, in line with overseas trends, is inevitable."
New technology had encouraged competitors, such as AMP's Ergo, to enter the market using telephone banking.
Dinsdale said New Zealand had 17 registered banks in 1996, the highest number since 1990, and it was possible Asian and European banks could set up here in future.
Total bank lending rose from $76 billion to $89 billion last year, but profits rose only slightly -- from $979 million to $995 million -- a 1.7 percent increase.
Fierce competition in the banking sector had kept pressure on profit margins, he said.
Banks would look to reduce costs in future as competition meant the opportunity to increase profits from business growth was limited. Staff numbers were down 1072 to 26,030.
Dinsdale said the year 2000 computer problem had the potential to cost banks millions of dollars.
For most institutions, preparing for the year 2000 was the single, most complex project ever attempted, he said.
